newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Round-world balloon bid aborted after six hours.
newsitem.headline: Round-world balloon bid aborted after six hours.

text.p: A bid by a Swiss doctor and a Belgian businessman to become the first men to fly round the world non-stop by balloon was aborted after six hours on Sunday when fumes leaked into their cabin.

Bertrand Piccard, from a family of explorers of the stratosphere and the ocean depths, and Wim Verstraeten, an experienced balloonist, were reported in good health after being picked from the sea off the south of France.

"Obviously, we are very, very sad," flight official Alan Noble, a Briton, told Reuters Television at mission control at Geneva airport as his disappointed team waited to be able to speak to Piccard and Verstraeten.

British businessman Richard Branson, who came to see the pair off after cutting short his own round-the-world attempt 24 hours into the flight last week, said in London he felt "incredibly sorry" for them but delighted they were safe.

Branson told Reuters he would now try again, probably in November this year. Another long-time balloonist, American millionaire Steve Fossett, is due to make his own bid in the next few days from St Louis, Missouri.

After a perfect lift-off from the Swiss Alpine ballooning centre of Chateau d'Oex just before 9 a.m. (0800 GMT) in blue skies and perfect flight conditions, hopes had been high for Piccard and Verstraeten's 40,000 km (25,000 mile) voyage.

"Anyone who was there will know it was such a beautiful sight," said Noble, whose company was responsible for logistical support for the planned 15-day venture aboard the British-built Breitling Orbiter.

But problems hit three hours out over France after the balloon had soared over the peaks of Mont Blanc when kerosene fumes leaked into the sealed and pressurised gondola-cabin from which the two were guiding the helium-filled balloon.
Noble said mission control told them by radio to bring the Orbiter down low enough for the roof of the canary yellow cabin to be opened safely.

"At first we thought the fumes would disperse and they could go on. But they said they felt so ill they couldn't continue." He said they were told to come down in the Mediterranean and the French naval and coast guard authorities were alerted.

Noble said the pair, who together won the first trans-Atlantic balloon race in 1992, brought the Orbiter for a "perfect touchdown" in the bay beyond the walled French medieval port town of Aigues Mortes.

They decided not to jettison the 45-metre (150 feet) high nylon balloon's protective aluminium cover, which Noble said would mean it could be easier to recover the whole craft intact and prepare it for another try at the end of the year.

But the deflated Orbiter partly covered the capsule, making it impossible for a rescue helicopter to lift them off. So a coastguard launch went out to retrieve the pair, who by then had emerged and were busy unhooking the capsule from the balloon.

Noble said both, who said goodbye to their wives and families in emotional early morning scenes before takeoff, would undergo medical checkups at the French coastal town of La Grande Motte and probably return to Geneva on Monday.

Piccard, a 38-year-old psychiatrist whose grandfather was the first man to take a balloon into the stratosphere, and Verstraeten, a 39-year-old pilot and businessman, had aimed to complete their circle of the globe in some 15 days.

They were planning to make use of the jet-stream air current that flow eastwards between the 30th and 40th parallels North to take them across Turkey, China, the Pacific Ocean and the United States back to Europe.
"It is not the first bid, and it will not be the last," said one member of the mission team. "Some day, someone is going to make it."
